History:
- Chief complaint: Sudden-onset severe headache with visual disturbance.
- Onset/duration: Began this morning, approximately 4 hours before consult; came on suddenly; persistent.
- Location/character: Left-sided headache; not clearly behind the eye; patient rates pain ~6/10 (kidney stone was 10/10).
- Associated symptoms: Blurred vision with “zigzag lines”; dizziness; nausea; vomited twice (at onset); worsens with movement; cannot tolerate screens.
- Alleviating/aggravating: Paracetamol taken ~3 hours ago without relief; prefers keeping head still.
- Previous episodes: None like this before.
- Patient concerns: Worried about serious causes (tumor or stroke).
- Pregnancy: Patient doubts possibility.

Past Medical History:
- Kidney stones (history).
- Medications: Paracetamol taken for current headache (dose/route/frequency not documented). No regular medications.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies per patient.
- Family history: Mother with migraines; family history of hypothyroidism.
- Social history: Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- No formal physical exam performed (teleconsult).
- Patient-reported findings: No limb weakness; able to walk in a straight line; ongoing visual disturbance; ongoing nausea; two episodes of vomiting.

Impression:
- Acute left-sided headache with visual aura, nausea, and vomiting—suspected migraine (first episode).

Management Plan:
- Trial symptomatic therapy: ibuprofen plus an anti-sickness medication obtainable from pharmacy (specific agent/dose not documented).
- Advice to drink a sugary, carbonated beverage (e.g., cola) as part of initial management.
- Arrange same-day in-person assessment for full neurological examination.
- If medications are effective and patient feels much better by appointment time, patient may call to cancel.
- Safety net: If any further problems before the appointment, contact the clinic.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with new, sudden-onset left-sided headache accompanied by visual aura, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. No focal neurological deficits reported. Clinical impression is a first episode migraine; initial pharmacy-based management advised and same-day in-person neuro exam arranged.

Key Takeaways:
- Start ibuprofen with an anti-sickness medication and a sugary carbonated drink now.
- Attend the same-day in-person assessment for a full neurological check, unless symptoms substantially improve—then call to cancel.
- Contact the clinic if symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop before the appointment.

Next Steps:
- In-person neurological examination today.
- If inadequate relief, consider escalation to specific migraine therapies (names/doses not documented in consult).

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vitals, formal neurological examination, red-flag screening (fever, neck stiffness, recent head trauma, exertional onset, anticoagulant use, jaw/temporal symptoms, immunosuppression), menstrual/contraceptive history, pregnancy test, detailed medication reconciliation, hydration/caffeine/sleep triggers.
- Internal conflicts: Clinician repeated “hyperthyroid,” patient clarified hypothyroidism in family—recorded as hypothyroidism (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Minor connectivity issues and brief interruptions; overall history understandable.
